# Interviewer guide — semantic search round trip

## Source

Real commit: `324ee36ca` -- "refactor: reduce semantic search overhead (#1128)".
Touches:

- `apps/backend/src/modules/catalog/catalog-cache.ts` (exports `getCachedCatalog`,
  previously module-private)
- `apps/backend/src/modules/catalog/controller.ts` (`getCatalogWithSemanticSearch`)
- `apps/backend/src/modules/semantic-search/client.ts` and
  `apps/backend/src/modules/semantic-search/controller.ts`
- `apps/semantic-search/app/engine.py` (the Python microservice)

Before the fix: the semantic search path called the Python microservice,
which returned `subject`, `courseNumber`, `title`, `description`, `score`,
and `text` for each match, then the backend did `CatalogClassModel.find()`
against MongoDB to fetch the *same* matching documents again -- even though
`catalog-cache.ts` already held a warm, TTL-refreshed, in-memory copy of the
exact same collection for the plain (non-semantic) fuzzy-search path. Every
semantic-search request paid for both a cross-service HTTP round trip and an
unnecessary DB hit a cache hit could have served for free.

After the fix: the Python service returns only `subject` + `courseNumber`
(stripped title/description/score/text -- nothing downstream needed them),
and the backend hydrates matches from `getCachedCatalog(year, semester)`
(now exported) instead of hitting Mongo again. `applyInMemoryFilters` runs
against the in-memory matches instead of being pushed into the Mongo query.

This question models the same shape at a smaller scale, generalized away
from Mongo/catalog specifics so candidates reason about the pattern, not
BT's schema.

## Round 1 discussion guide

Use the four angles below as your rubric for what a strong candidate covers.
Don't present #1 as "the" answer going in -- see which of these the
candidate reaches on their own, and push on the ones they skip.

**1. External service returns ids only; hydrate from the existing warm cache
(what BT shipped).**
Fast (no second network/DB call), and correct as long as the cache is
trustworthy and fresh for every field the client needs. The dependency this
creates: the semantic search path is now coupled to the cache's freshness
guarantees, which were previously only load-bearing for the plain search
path. If the cache's TTL or invalidation logic ever has a bug, semantic
search silently inherits it.

**2. External service returns full denormalized objects itself.**
Removes the backend hydration step entirely -- the ranking service becomes
self-sufficient. Cost: the ranking service needs its own copy/replica of the
full dataset, which means two copies of the same data can drift (the
embedding index rebuilds on its own schedule; the OLTP data changes
independently). Also pushes payload size and schema-coupling onto the
external service, which now must track backend schema changes.

**3. "Hydrate from cache, fall back to DB on cache miss" wrapper.**
Resilient to partial cache staleness/gaps -- e.g. the cache holds N of the M
matched ids because of an eviction, cold key, or race with a refresh. Slightly
more complex (two code paths, need to decide batching strategy for the
fallback), but strictly more robust than #1 with no meaningful latency cost
if the fallback path is rare. This is what the `impl/` project asks
candidates to implement, because it's the version that has an interesting
extra edge (see below) that a naive "just add a cache read" fix will still
get wrong.

**4. Cache the semantic-search RESULTS themselves (query -> ranked id list).**
A different, complementary optimization -- it would skip the ranking
service round trip entirely for repeated/popular queries, but does nothing
about the original redundant-hydration bug by itself (you could cache the
ranking call and still redundantly hit the DB to hydrate every time). Good
candidates raise this as a "also worth doing, doesn't replace #1/#3" point,
not a substitute.

### Follow-ups

- "What if the in-memory cache had a bug and was slightly stale for one
  field the semantic search result needs (say, `units`, and a unit count
  changed after the cache was last warmed) -- how would you catch that class
  of bug, and does your design make it more or less likely to surface, versus
  the old always-hit-the-DB design?" Looking for: acknowledgment that
  hydration-from-cache trades a small, bounded staleness window (bounded by
  the cache's TTL) for latency, and that this tradeoff already exists
  latently for the plain search path today -- it's not new risk introduced by
  the fix, it's newly *shared* risk. Bonus: mentioning tests/monitoring that
  would catch cache/DB drift (e.g. a periodic consistency check, or logging
  when a cache-hydrated field disagrees with a DB spot-check).
- "Where would you draw the line on which fields are safe to serve from a
  TTL'd cache vs. which need to always be fresh?" Looking for: recognizing
  that this is about the specific fields the *client* consumes and how
  sensitive they are to staleness (e.g. seat availability/enrollment counts
  are more staleness-sensitive than a course title), not a blanket
  cache-everything-or-nothing stance.
- "Suppose the ranking service starts returning 10x more results per query.
  Does your design still hold up?" Looking for: batching consideration for
  the cache-miss fallback path (option 3), and whether cache lookups are
  O(1) per id (map/dict) vs. something that degrades.

### Red flags

- Doesn't ask whether a cache already exists for this data before designing
  a fix -- just assumes "call the DB to hydrate" is normal/expected instead
  of treating a second full-record fetch as suspicious given a ranking
  service that only returns ids.
- Proposes cache-hydration (option 1 or 3) with zero discussion of
  staleness risk, i.e., presents it as strictly free.
- Conflates "cache the catalog data" (option 1/3) with "cache the search
  results" (option 4) as if they're the same optimization solving the same
  problem.
- Can't articulate why the external ranking service can't just be the
  source of full records too (i.e., doesn't reach option 2's
  duplication/staleness tradeoff on their own, even after a nudge).

## Round 2 code review guide

### What the test suite checks

`impl/test/semanticSearch.test.ts` has two describe blocks. Since
`semanticSearch` ships as a stub that unconditionally throws, all 8 tests
fail on an untouched starter -- that's expected and not itself informative;
what matters is which ones a candidate's implementation ends up passing.

- **Correctness** (4 tests): for a correct implementation, hydrated fields
  must be right and in rank order for an all-cache-hit query
  ("intro to programming"), a genuine-cache-miss query
  ("probability theory", where `STAT-134-001` must come from the `dbLookup`
  fallback since it isn't in `catalogCache`), a query with an id that
  resolves in neither the cache nor the "DB" ("web development", where
  `COMPSCI-999-001` must be dropped rather than thrown or left as a hole),
  and an empty-result query ("medieval basket weaving" -> `[]`).
- **Avoids the redundant DB round-trip** (4 tests): for a correct
  implementation, `getDbLookupCallCount()` must be `0` on the all-cache-hit
  and empty-result queries, and exactly `1` on both the cache-miss query and
  the double-miss query -- with `getDbLookupCallArgs()` showing that single
  call was scoped to *only* the missing id(s) (e.g. `["STAT-134-001"]`), not
  the full ranked list. These are the tests that distinguish a genuinely
  cache-first implementation from one that still round-trips to the DB for
  everything, or that batches incorrectly.

The fixtures bake in one deliberate cache-miss case (`STAT-134-001`, ranked
by the mock service for the "probability theory" query but absent from
`catalogCache`) specifically so that an implementation that never calls
`dbLookup` at all also fails -- the fallback path needs to actually work. A
second fixture (`COMPSCI-999-001`, "web development" query) resolves in
neither the cache nor the DB, to check the candidate's implementation
doesn't crash or leak an `undefined` into the results on a double-miss.

### Reference solution sketch

This is one correct approach, not the only one -- use it as a comparison
point, not a checklist. A candidate's implementation may structure the
cache/miss bookkeeping differently (e.g. two arrays instead of a `Map`) and
still be fully correct.

```ts
export async function semanticSearch(query: string): Promise<ClassRecord[]> {
  const rankedIds = semanticSearchService.rank(query);
  if (rankedIds.length === 0) return [];

  const hydrated = new Map<string, ClassRecord>();
  const misses: string[] = [];

  for (const id of rankedIds) {
    const cached = catalogCache.get(id);
    if (cached) hydrated.set(id, cached);
    else misses.push(id);
  }

  if (misses.length > 0) {
    const fetched = await dbLookup(misses); // single batched fallback call
    for (const record of fetched) hydrated.set(record.classId, record);
  }

  return rankedIds
    .map((id) => hydrated.get(id))
    .filter((r): r is ClassRecord => Boolean(r));
}
```

Key properties: cache-first per id, one batched `dbLookup` call scoped to
misses only (never zero-arg, never the full ranked list "just in case"),
missing-everywhere ids silently filtered, order preserved by iterating
`rankedIds` at the end rather than sorting whatever `dbLookup`/cache
returned.

### AI-tool-usage questions to ask

- "Walk me through a prompt you used. What did the model produce first, and
  did you change anything before accepting it?"
- "Did the AI's first draft default to a cache-first approach on its own, or
  did it default to always calling `dbLookup` and hydrating from there?" If
  the latter: "how did you catch that, and what did you change?" -- gauges
  whether the candidate understood the contract well enough to notice a
  plausible-looking-but-wrong first draft, rather than shipping whatever the
  model produced.
- If they used AI to generate the whole implementation in one shot: "did you
  verify it actually avoids calling `dbLookup` on the happy path, or just
  that the tests were green?" (Green tests and a correct understanding are
  not the same thing -- probe whether they'd have caught a subtly-wrong
  batching strategy, e.g. one `dbLookup` call per missing id instead of one
  batched call, since that also makes the count-based tests pass in some
  configurations but fails the call-args assertion.)

### Red flags

- **The big one:** candidate's implementation returns correct data but still
  calls `dbLookup` for every id (e.g., they wrote a correctness-only pass --
  rank, then hydrate everything via `dbLookup` -- without ever reading from
  `catalogCache` first, or they read the cache only to validate/overwrite
  what `dbLookup` already returned). This means they satisfied the
  correctness half of the contract without noticing the redundancy
  requirement was the actual point. Probe explicitly: "why does the contract
  ask for cache-first hydration, in your own words?" A candidate who can't
  answer this crisply, even if their diff happens to pass tests, hasn't
  understood the exercise.
- Never calls `dbLookup` at all and doesn't notice the cache-miss test now
  fails (or worse, edits the test/fixtures to make it pass).
- Batches incorrectly -- calls `dbLookup` once per missing id in a loop
  instead of one call with all missing ids -- and doesn't notice
  `getDbLookupCallArgs()` catches this even when `getDbLookupCallCount()`
  might coincidentally still look reasonable for a single-miss fixture.
- Edits `dbLookup.ts`'s instrumentation, the fixtures, or the test file to
  make things pass, rather than implementing `semanticSearch.ts` correctly.
- No AI-prompt log brought to review despite clearly having used AI-generated
  code (inconsistent style/comments relative to their own code, or an
  implementation that doesn't match how they talk about it).

## Rubric (1-5 each)

| Dimension | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| System design judgment | Doesn't spot the redundancy without heavy prompting; treats a fresh DB call as normal | Identifies the redundancy and proposes cache hydration, but design is vague on the miss/fallback case | Designs a complete data flow (cache-first, scoped fallback, handles double-miss) and reasons about which fields are cache-safe |
| Code quality/correctness | Implementation doesn't compile/pass tests, or "passes" by editing tests/fixtures | Passes correctness tests but fails or only partially satisfies the call-count/call-args tests | All 8 tests pass; fallback is a single batched call scoped to genuine misses; handles the double-miss case cleanly |
| Tradeoff articulation | Presents one option as free/obviously correct with no downsides | Names 2 of the 4 design angles (cache-only, full-replica, fallback wrapper, result-caching) with basic tradeoffs | Covers most/all 4 angles unprompted, and correctly separates "cache the data" from "cache the search results" as distinct optimizations |
| AI-tool usage judgment | No log, or log shows blind accept-all of generated code with no verification | Has a log; can describe what was accepted/rejected at a high level | Log shows targeted prompts, clear description of what was verified/rejected, and can explain *why* a subtly-wrong AI suggestion (e.g. per-id fallback calls) would or wouldn't pass the test suite |
| Communication | Can't explain their own implementation's behavior when asked | Explains the implementation correctly but not fluently under follow-up questions | Clearly explains both the contract's requirements and their implementation's behavior, including edge cases, without prompting |

## Time budget

- Round 1: 45-60 min. ~10 min framing the problem, ~30-40 min design
  discussion across the 4 angles + follow-ups, ~5-10 min buffer/questions.
- Round 2: 3-4 hours, done independently (take-home or proctored block).
  Code review session afterward: 30-45 min, covering the reference-solution
  comparison, AI-tool-usage questions, and rubric scoring above.
